scholarly_quality.concise_summary: The study presents a clear, well-scoped system that addresses a well-identified failure mode of flat memory in test-time continual learning. The methodology is thoroughly detailed, formal bounds are derived, and empirical results demonstrate substantial token and training-time efficiency gains on objective external tasks.

• GraphMemory.We introduce GRAPHMEMORY, a lightweight external memory that
accumulates, refines, organizes, and connects reusable strategies in an evolving graph. Nodes
represent ACE-style knowledge points, while weighted edges capture useful relationships
among them. For each query, GraphMemory identifies relevant entry nodes, traverses their
local neighborhoods, and supplies only the resulting subgraph to the language model. This
replaces full-memory prompting with selective relational retrieval while preserving the
interpretability, portability, and weight-free adaptation of natural-language memory.

We use ACE as our workhorse for realizing GraphMemory. GraphMemory changes ACE at precisely
two interfaces: what the Generator (f) reads and what the Curator (O) writes. Instead of exposing
the complete playbook to every query, we prepend a retrieval stage; instead of writing only bullet-
point updates, the Curator can also write relations between them. The resulting adaptation loop is
RETRIEVE–GENERATE–REFLECT–CURATE, as illustrated in Figure 2. For retrieval, we maintain a
compact index containing each node's identifier and a short key, but not its full bullet-point content.

deterministic breadth-first traversal from those entries, expanding neighbors in order of learned edge

evidence.excerpt:
time. Training
time decreases by 21.0% on FORMULA(6.4 versus 8.1 hours) and 34.3% on FINER (19.0 versus
28.9 hours). GraphMemory is slower during inference, however, requiring approximately 1.8 ×
as much time per test example. This overhead arises because GraphMemory performs retrieval
before generating each prediction, whereas ACE directly supplies its complete memory to the
backbone. A more efficient implementation ofϕ, such as an embedding-based retriever, could reduce
inference latency and further decrease training time. We leave this investigation to future work. Thus,
GraphMemory trades a modest increase in per-query latency for substantially lower context length,
training cost, and test-time token consumption.

financial tasks and two LLM backbones, GraphMemory remains competitive
with ACE while reducing memory-construction tokens by 81–85%, test-time tokens by 79–92%,
and estimated API cost similarly. Learning trajectories suggest slower initial adaptation but greater
stability and continued improvement.
Our results remain preliminary, covering two related tasks, two models, and one primary baseline.
Broader evaluations, additional memory and prompt-optimization baselines, and repeated runs are
needed. Retrieval overhead also makes individual test queries slower despite lower token usage,
motivating embedding-based and hybrid retrievers, caching, and improved graph routing. Finally,
longer continual-learning streams and cross-model transfer will test whether improvements persist
beyond one epoch and whether memory built by larger models can efficiently adapt smaller ones.

evidence.excerpt:
Retrieval has two stages. First, an LLM Retriever reads the compact index and returns a structured
selection of up to two index sections and at most six entry nodes. Second, GraphMemory performs
a weight-prioritized breadth-first traversal over outgoing edges. Entry nodes have depth zero. At
each breadth level, active outgoing neighbors are ordered by decreasing posterior-mean weight from
Equation (19), with target-node identifier used as a deterministic tie-break, and at most the two
highest-scoring neighbors of a loaded node are considered. Traversal is bounded by two hops from
each entry node, at most 12 loaded nodes, and at most 2,500 tokens of serialized node content. A
node is not loaded if doing so would violate either the node or token budget.

a weight-prioritized breadth-first traversal over outgoing edges. Entry nodes have depth zero. At
each breadth level, active outgoing neighbors are ordered by decreasing posterior-mean weight from
Equation (19), with target-node identifier used as a deterministic tie-break, and at most the two
highest-scoring neighbors of a loaded node are considered. Traversal is bounded by two hops from
each entry node, at most 12 loaded nodes, and at most 2,500 tokens of serialized node content. A
node is not loaded if doing so would violate either the node or token budget.

examples,
ct =ϕ(G (t),xt),by t =f(c t,xt).(22)
Only after producingbyt does the Reflector inspect the prediction, available feedback, and execution
trace. The Curator then emits local graph edits, which are applied to obtainG(t+1). Consequently,
information derived fromyt cannot affect the prediction onxt; it becomes available only to subsequent
examples. The Generator and Reflector retain ACE's core roles, with the additional memory-use
tracing and edge feedback described above, while the Retriever and graph-valued Curator implement
the two GraphMemory-specific interfaces described in Section 3.

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: Held-out test accuracy on FORMULA and FINER is measured against ground-truth labels, independent of the Reflector feedback used to shape graph edges and nodes.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Held-out test accuracy on FORMULA and FINER, selected by best validation checkpoint.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: LLM Reflector helpful/harmful/neutral transition labels and ACE-style critique that drive Curator node and edge updates.

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: The headline claims that GraphMemory achieves competitive task accuracy while reducing memory-construction tokens by 81-85% and test tokens by 79-92% are directly supported by the reported empirical tables. Authors clearly document trade-offs, such as higher per-query test latency and modest accuracy drops relative to uncapped or high-cap flat memory.
primary.evaluation_assessment: Experiments compare GraphMemory against ACE on two financial reasoning datasets (FORMULA and FiNER) across two LLM backbones (Claude Haiku 4.5 and Qwen3.8-27B) using held-out test splits. Metrics include objective downstream accuracy, cumulative training and test token counts, estimated monetary cost, and active wall-clock time.

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: Downstream task performance is measured against ground-truth labels on held-out test splits rather than by internal reflective feedback.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Objective downstream task accuracy on held-out test sets of financial benchmark datasets (FORMULA and FiNER).
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: An LLM Reflector generates qualitative critique and transition feedback (helpful/harmful/neutral) that guides the Curator in updating graph nodes and edge weights.

primary.limitations: The manuscript acknowledges limitations including the small number of tasks (two financial domains), evaluation against only one primary baseline (ACE), single-run evaluation without repeated trials, and the fact that reading the index retains residual growth rather than strict end-to-end O(1) complexity.
primary.method_assessment: The architecture extends Agentic Context Engineering (ACE) to a Retrieve-Generate-Reflect-Curate loop, updating node context and edge transition weights modeled as Beta posterior distributions over helpful/harmful reflective feedback. Retrieval constraints (depth, maximum nodes, and token limits) are clearly defined and accompanied by formal scaling properties.
primary.quality_rationale: The study presents a clear, well-scoped system that addresses a well-identified failure mode of flat memory in test-time continual learning. The methodology is thoroughly detailed, formal bounds are derived, and empirical results demonstrate substantial token and training-time efficiency gains on objective external tasks.
primary.scoped_contribution: The paper formalizes context adaptation as optimization and introduces GraphMemory, a graph-structured external natural language memory that selectively retrieves relevant subgraphs using an LLM retriever and breadth-first search to reduce token usage during test-time continual adaptation.

scholarly_quality.rationale: The study presents a clear, well-scoped system that addresses a well-identified failure mode of flat memory in test-time continual learning. The methodology is thoroughly detailed, formal bounds are derived, and empirical results demonstrate substantial token and training-time efficiency gains on objective external tasks.
scholarly_quality.uncertainty: The manuscript acknowledges limitations including the small number of tasks (two financial domains), evaluation against only one primary baseline (ACE), single-run evaluation without repeated trials, and the fact that reading the index retains residual growth rather than strict end-to-end O(1) complexity.
